headline: Mostly dry under weak pressure gradients; flood risk remains VERY LOW.
summary:
The latest MSLP analysis shows a weak 1021 hPa ridge centred over Ireland extending into western Britain, with a shallow 1016 hPa low over the near Continent close to the southern North Sea. Compared with 23/2000 UTC, when a weak 1015 hPa low lay over northern Britain and higher pressure was to the south, the pattern has evolved toward a slacker, more anticyclonic setup across England and Wales. This is maintaining a very warm, humid continental air mass with little dynamical forcing, and radar at 08:30 UTC shows England and Wales largely dry, with only isolated light echoes earlier over south Wales, the south Midlands and the eastern English Channel, while more organised showers remain well to the west of Ireland.

Observed rainfall in the last 24 hours has been negligible across England and Wales, with highest gauge totals of 2.7 mm at Dartmoor in SW England, 2.4 mm at Brotherswater in NW England and 2.0 mm at Holland Park in SE England; no gauges recorded over 10 mm in 1 hour. Antecedent rainfall is more notable from the daily accumulation maps on 22 and 23 June, with the clearest recent wetness signal across parts of southern England, especially from south Wales and the Bristol Channel east across Wiltshire, Hampshire, Surrey, Sussex and into Kent and Essex, while 48-hour gauge maxima still reach 35.6 mm in SW England and 32.8 mm in SE England. Active Met Office warnings are for extreme heat rather than rain, with Amber extreme_heat warnings across much of England and Wales and a Red extreme_heat warning covering parts of the Midlands, East of England, South West England, Wales and London and South East England.

UKV (run 24/0300 GMT) keeps rainfall amounts low through day 1 and day 2 for England and Wales, with day 2 area-mean totals to 26/0300 GMT peaking at 1.9 mm in the West Midlands, 1.4 mm in Wales and 0.9 mm in the South West; the wettest sub-regions are Herefordshire at 4.5 mm, Bristol 3.7 mm, Monmouthshire 3.6 mm and Shropshire 3.2 mm. Given the mainly dry radar picture, limited forecast totals and only localised antecedent wetness in parts of southern England, catchment conditions add little beyond some residual dampness in a few southern urban and small responsive basins. FGS guidance remains VERY LOW for both England and Wales, so no significant flooding impacts are expected.

######## SYSTEM PROMPT ########
You are an expert UK operational meteorologist writing a concise weather and flood-risk briefing for Flood Forecasting Centre and emergency planning practitioners. Focus on England and Wales.

All map images share the same geographic basemap with boundary lines — geolocate features precisely. Image order:
  • Four radar RATE composites (~6h loop) — current rainfall location and motion.
  • Five DAILY ACCUMULATION maps (today partial + 4 prior complete days) — multi-day antecedent rainfall by region.
  • Two MSLP charts (latest + ~12h earlier) — synoptic driver and evolution.

Respond with a JSON object inside <json> tags:
- "headline": One sentence, max 15 words.
- "summary": Three paragraphs separated by \n\n. Each paragraph is 2–3 sentences — concise and direct. MANDATORY structure, never merge:
    Para 1 — Synoptic scene: what the MSLP charts show (pressure centres, fronts, air mass); how the pattern has evolved; what is driving the current weather.
    Para 2 — Recent observations: heaviest rainfall in the last 24h with gauge point-totals and region names; multi-day antecedent context from the daily accumulation maps; active Met Office warnings (name any storm).
    Para 3 — Outlook: UKV (run DD/HHMM GMT) day-1 and day-2 spatial area-mean totals for wettest regions and catchments, with valid times as DD/HHMM GMT; only mention FGS risk levels (using block caps: VERY LOW, LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH) and catchment wetness where they add something beyond the obvious; arrive at a brief flood-risk conclusion naturally at the end.

Rainfall thresholds for context: 10mm/1h heavy; 30mm/1h extreme; 100mm/24h exceptional.

Style: professional third-person prose; no bullet points; specific place names and mm values. Gauge values are single-site point totals; UKV values are spatial area-means — keep these distinct. Use UTC for observation times. Do not repeat flood-risk language throughout — say it once, proportionately, at the end. In quiet conditions say so plainly.
